nodes.name: Continuous-time random walk with drift
nodes.statement:
By this we understand a
random process $X_t$ whose evolution in

nodes.name: Drifting CTRW process X_t
nodes.statement:
Thus,  for $t\geqslant t_0$ we define
\begin{equation}
X_t=X_{t_0}+v(t-t_0)+S_{t}, \quad S_t=\sum_{n=1}^\infty J_n\
\theta(t-t_n), \end{equation}
where $\theta(u)=1$ for $u \geqslant 0$,
$t_n=\tau_1+\cdots+\tau_n$ are the jump  times,  $J_n$ the

nodes.statement_short: Defines $X_t$ as initial value plus linear drift $vt$ plus the jump sum $S_t$ with jump times $t_n$ and sizes $J_n$.

nodes.name: i.i.d. sojourn times and jumps
nodes.statement:
All through this paper  we will assume that (i) the
sojourn times $\tau_n>0$
 are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables with
probability density and cumulative distribution function (PDF and,
respectively, CDF) $\psi(t)$ and $\Psi(t)=  \int_0^t \psi(t')d
t'$; (ii) $\{J_n\}$ is a sequence of i.i.d. random variables  with
common PDF $h(\cdot)$; and  (iii), that  $ J_m$ is independent of $\tau_n $ for any $n,m$.
nodes.statement_short: Sojourn times i.i.d. with PDF $\psi$ and CDF $\Psi$; jumps i.i.d. with PDF $h$; jumps independent of sojourn times.

nodes.name: Compound Poisson process
nodes.statement:
In absence of drift, and when  the holding times $\tau_n$ are exponentially distributed, $\tau_n\sim  \mathcal  E(\lambda)$ for some $\lambda >0$, the jump process  $S_t$ is  a  classical compound Poisson process (CPP)
characterized by having     independent increments  $S_{t+h}- S_t$; in addition the
    associated  ``arrival-process''   $N_t\equiv\sum_{n=1}^\infty \theta(t-t_n)$  is
  Poisson
 distributed:   $N_t \sim
\mathcal P(\lambda
 t)$.
nodes.statement_short: With exponential holding times and no drift, $S_t$ is a compound Poisson process and the arrival process $N_t$ is Poisson.

nodes.name: Exit time after the present and its mean
nodes.statement:
To this  end    let $r+\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$ be the first time past
$r$ at which $X_t$ exits $(0,b)$;   $T_{b}(x,r)$ be its expected
value:

nodes.name: Mean exit time after a jump
nodes.statement:
$T_{b}(x,r) =\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}]$; finally let
$\mathbb{T}_{b}(x) $ denote   the mean exit time   off $(0,b)$     after
a jump $t_n$ (loosely one has $\mathbb{T}_{b}(x)=T_{b}(x,t_n), n=0,\dots,
\infty$; however the relation between both   quantities is not
trivial, as we see below in Section~\ref{S_up}).
nodes.statement_short: $T_b(x,r)$ is the mean of $\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$; $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$ is the mean exit time from $(0,b)$ after a jump.

nodes.name: Markov case: exit time independent of present time
nodes.statement:
In the exponential Markov case    $
\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$ is independent of $r$, $T_{b}(x,r)=\mathbb{T}_{b}(x)$
and it \it only \rm remains to formulate (and solve) the equation
that  this object satisfies.

nodes.name: Excess life
nodes.statement:
We find (see below and
Section~\ref{S_up}) that  the relation between $T_{b}(x,r)$ and
$\mathbb{T}_{b}(x)$ involves     the  ``excess life'' $E_r\equiv
t_{N_r+1}-r$, or time elapsed   until  the next arrival    occurs.

nodes.name: CDF of the excess life
nodes.statement:
We  now  sketch classical renewal theory (see \cite{kt81,c65}
 and  \cite{Go}) that
   shows how to construct  the CDF    $\Phi(t|r)\equiv
\Bbb P\{E_r\leqslant t\}$ of $E_r$.

nodes.name: Derivation of the driftless correction
nodes.statement:
Indeed  let $t_{N_r}\equiv t_n$, say,  be the ``last'' jump time
   and  $E_r^-  \equiv r- t_n$     the time elapsed
  from  $t_n$     to the present. Then, with $E_r^+\equiv
 E_r$ one  obviously has that
 $E_r^-+E_r^+=t_{n+1}-t_n\equiv\tau_{n+1}$, and that the exit time right
after $t_n$ is that after $r$, $\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$,  plus $E_r^-$, and hence
 \begin{equation}\mathbb{T}_{b}(x)=\mathbb{E} [E_r^-]+
\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}]=\mathbb{E}[\tau_{n+1}]-\mathbb{E}[E_r^+]+
T_{b}(x,r). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Split the last inter-jump interval into backward and forward recurrence times; the exit time after the jump equals that after $r$ plus $E_r^-$.

nodes.name: Driftless relation between exit times
nodes.statement:
\mathbb{T}_{b}(x)=\mathbb{E} [E_r^-]+
\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}]=\mathbb{E}[\tau_{n+1}]-\mathbb{E}[E_r^+]+
T_{b}(x,r).
nodes.label: v=0

nodes.name: Driftless correction depends only on r
nodes.statement:
Thus,
 $T_{b}(x,r)
 $   follows    adding a   correction     term to $\mathbb{T}_{b}(x)$ which  depends only on $r$.
conclusions: $T_{b}(x,r) $ follows adding a correction term to $\mathbb{T}_{b}(x)$ which depends only on $r$

nodes.name: Favorable drift: positive drift and jumps
nodes.statement:
In this section we consider the case when both drift and jumps
have a positive sign, i.e. when $X_t$ is increasing.

nodes.name: Renewal argument for favorable drift
nodes.statement:
Let us assume that at time $t=r$ the system is in $X_r=x\in(0,b)$, and that the excess life $E_r$ is known in advance, $E_r=l$. If the excess life is longer than $\varrho \equiv {b-x\over v}< l$, the drift will drive the process
out of the region at time $r+\varrho$, before the next jump takes place at $t_{N_r+1}$. Conversely, if $l \leqslant \varrho$ at least a jump of size $J_{N_r+1}=u$ will occur prior to exiting the interval. Note that just before $t_{N_r+1}$ the process $X_t$ is no longer at $x$, but at $x+v l$. Therefore, two possible scenarios appear: either
the jump size is larger than the remaining distance up to the upper boundary, $u\geqslant b-x-v l$, and the process leaves the
interval at $r+E_r$, 
or it does not. In the latter case the problem renews from $t=r+l$, $X_{r+l}=x+v
l+u$, so the mean escape time will be increased by an amount $\mathbb{T}_b\left(x+v
l+u\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Condition on the excess life $E_r=l$: exit by drift if $l>\varrho$, else a jump either exits or renews the problem at $x+vl+u$.

nodes.name: Drift time to the boundary rho
nodes.statement:
If the excess life is longer than $\varrho \equiv {b-x\over v}< l$, the drift will drive the process
out of the region at time $r+\varrho$, before the next jump takes place at $t_{N_r+1}$.

nodes.name: Excess life beyond rho
nodes.statement:
Let us assume that at time $t=r$ the system is in $X_r=x\in(0,b)$, and that the excess life $E_r$ is known in advance, $E_r=l$. If the excess life is longer than $\varrho \equiv {b-x\over v}< l$, the drift will drive the process
out of the region at time $r+\varrho$, before the next jump takes place at $t_{N_r+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $X_r=x$, $E_r=l$; if $l>\varrho$ the drift exits before the next jump.

nodes.name: Jump before exit
nodes.statement: Conversely, if $l \leqslant \varrho$ at least a jump of size $J_{N_r+1}=u$ will occur prior to exiting the interval. Note that just before $t_{N_r+1}$ the process $X_t$ is no longer at $x$, but at $x+v l$.
nodes.statement_short: If $l\le\varrho$ a jump occurs, from position $x+vl$.

nodes.name: Jump exits or renews
nodes.statement:
Therefore, two possible scenarios appear: either
the jump size is larger than the remaining distance up to the upper boundary, $u\geqslant b-x-v l$, and the process leaves the
interval at $r+E_r$, 
or it does not. In the latter case the problem renews from $t=r+l$, $X_{r+l}=x+v
l+u$, so the mean escape time will be increased by an amount $\mathbb{T}_b\left(x+v
l+u\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: The jump either exits the interval or the problem renews from $x+vl+u$, adding $\mathbb{T}_b$.

nodes.name: Equation for T_b(x,r) with favorable drift
nodes.statement:
It can be proven that  these considerations imply
that $T_b(x,r)$ must satisfy |recall that $\psi(\cdot)$, $h(\cdot)$ are the
waiting-time and, respectively, jump PDFs| the following equation
\begin{eqnarray}
T_b(x,r)=\left[1-\Phi\left(\varrho|r\right)\right] \varrho +
\int^{\varrho}_{0} l
\phi(l|r) \int^{\infty}_{b-x-v l} h(u) d  ud  l\nonumber \\
+\int^{\varrho}_{0} \phi(l|r) \int^{b-x-v l}_{0} h(u)
\left[l+\mathbb{T}_b\left(x+vl+u\right)\right]d  ud  l, \end{eqnarray} an expression that relates $T_b(x,r)$ and $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: $T_b(x,r)$ satisfies an integral equation in the excess-life law $\Phi(\cdot|r)$, the jump PDF $h$ and $\mathbb{T}_b$.

nodes.name: Integral relation for T_b(x,r), favorable drift
nodes.statement:
T_b(x,r)=\left[1-\Phi\left(\varrho|r\right)\right] \varrho +
\int^{\varrho}_{0} l
\phi(l|r) \int^{\infty}_{b-x-v l} h(u) d  ud  l\nonumber \\
+\int^{\varrho}_{0} \phi(l|r) \int^{b-x-v l}_{0} h(u)
\left[l+\mathbb{T}_b\left(x+vl+u\right)\right]d  ud  l,
nodes.label: Tb_up0

nodes.name: Rearranged equation for T_b(x,r), favorable drift
nodes.statement:
T_b(x,r)= \int^{\varrho}_{0}\left[1-\Phi\left(l|r\right)\right]d
l \nonumber \\+ \frac{1}{v}\int^{v \varrho}_{0}
 \phi\left(\left.\varrho-\frac{z}{v}\right|r\right) \int^{z}_{0} h(u)
\mathbb{T}_b\left(b-z+u\right)d  u  d  z.
nodes.label: Tb_up

nodes.name: Integral equation for mean exit time after a jump, favorable drift
nodes.statement:
\mathbb{T}_b(x)= \int^{\varrho}_{0}\left[1-\Psi(l)\right]d  l  \nonumber \\
+\frac{1}{v}\int^{v \varrho}_{0}
\psi\left(\varrho-\frac{z}{v}\right) \int^{z}_{0} h(u)
\mathbb{T}_b\left(b-z+u\right)d  ud  z,
nodes.label: TTb_up

nodes.name: Reduction to the driftless equation
nodes.statement:
The second of these
  defines an  integral equation for $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$ which, if $v=0$,
 reduces upon appropriate change to that  of  \cite{mmp05,mmpw06}.

nodes.name: Explicit solvability of the favorable-drift equation
nodes.statement:
It is remarkable that Eq.~(\ref{TTb_up}) \it can be solved in a fully
explicit way.
conclusions: Eq.~(\ref{TTb_up}) \it can be solved in a fully explicit way

nodes.name: Allied function F(y)
nodes.statement:
To this end we define the    allied object
$\mathbb{F}(y)$, 
as the solution of the following integral
equation
\begin{eqnarray}
\mathbb{F}(y)= \int^{y/v}_{0}\left[1-\Psi(l)\right]d  l  \nonumber \\
+\frac{1}{v}\int^{y}_{0} \psi\left(\frac{y-z}{v}\right)
\int^{z}_{0} h(u) \mathbb{F}\left(z-u\right)d  ud  z, \end{eqnarray}
for $y\in \mathbb{R}^{+}$.
nodes.genus: solution of the following integral equation

nodes.name: Integral equation for F
nodes.statement:
\mathbb{F}(y)= \int^{y/v}_{0}\left[1-\Psi(l)\right]d  l  \nonumber \\
+\frac{1}{v}\int^{y}_{0} \psi\left(\frac{y-z}{v}\right)
\int^{z}_{0} h(u) \mathbb{F}\left(z-u\right)d  ud  z,
nodes.label: FF_eq

nodes.name: Mean exit time equals F(b-x)
nodes.statement:
Then it follows that $\mathbb{T}_b(x) =\mathbb{F}(b-x)$, for
$x\in (0,b)$.

nodes.name: Laplace transform of F
nodes.statement:
We note further that   taking a   Laplace
transformation in   Eq.~(\ref{FF_eq})  we    find that
\begin{equation}
\hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)= \frac{1}{v s^2}\frac{1-\hat{\psi}(s
v)}{1-\hat{\psi}(s v)\hat{h}(s)}, \end{equation}
where  $\hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)\equiv \int^{\infty}_{0} \mathbb{F}(y) e^{-s y}d y$,
$\hat{h}(s)\equiv \int^{\infty}_{0} h(u) e^{-s u}d  u$, and
$\hat{\psi}(s)\equiv \int^{\infty}_{0} \psi(s) e^{-s t}d  t$.
nodes.statement_short: Laplace transforming the equation for $\mathbb{F}$ gives $\hat{\mathbb{F}}$ in closed form in terms of $\hat\psi$ and $\hat h$.

nodes.name: Closed-form Laplace transform of F
nodes.statement:
\hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)= \frac{1}{v s^2}\frac{1-\hat{\psi}(s
v)}{1-\hat{\psi}(s v)\hat{h}(s)},

nodes.name: Laplace transform of the corrected mean exit time
nodes.statement:
Further, we also have
\begin{equation}
\hat{J}(s|r) =  \hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)-   \frac{ 1- \hat{h}(s) }{v
s^2\left[1-\hat{\psi}(s v)\hat{h}(s)\right]}\left[\hat{\phi}(s
v|r)-\hat{\psi}(s v )\right], \end{equation}
where the correction to the mean time after a jump is clearly
displayed and again, for convenience, we defined $J(y|r)\equiv T_b(b-y|r)$, and extended (\ref{Tb_up}) to $y\geqslant 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Closed-form Laplace transform of $J(y|r)=T_b(b-y|r)$: $\hat{\mathbb{F}}$ minus a correction involving $\hat\phi(\cdot|r)-\hat\psi$.

nodes.name: Laplace transform of J(y|r)
nodes.statement:
\hat{J}(s|r) =  \hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)-   \frac{ 1- \hat{h}(s) }{v
s^2\left[1-\hat{\psi}(s v)\hat{h}(s)\right]}\left[\hat{\phi}(s
v|r)-\hat{\psi}(s v )\right],
nodes.label: hattime

conclusions: $\hat{ J}(s|r)$ has an expansion in powers of $v$
nodes.statement_short: For small drift $v$, $\hat J(s|r)$ expands in powers of $v$, recovering the driftless relation.

\hat{J}(s|r) =  \hat{\mathbb{F}}(s) - \frac{\mu-\mu_r}{s}  -    \frac{
\hat{h}(s) }{ 1- \hat{h}(s) }   (\mu-\mu_r)\mu  v + O(v^2),

nodes.name: Steady-state limit r to infinity
nodes.statement:
Recalling that by the renewal theorem
$\underset{t\to\infty}\lim m(t)/t = 1/\mu$,  Eqs.~(\ref{hat_phi}) and~(\ref{hattime}) yield

nodes.name: Cramer-Lundberg model
nodes.statement:
The   resulting process  is
 a prototype  model in  risk management to describe   the
dynamics of the cahsflow  $X_t$ at an insurance company  under
the assumption  that premiums are received at a constant rate
$v>0$ and that  the company incurs in losses $J_n<0$
  from
claims reported at times $t_n, n=1,\dots\infty$   (the
Cramer-Lundberg model).

nodes.name: Renewal argument for opposite drift and jumps
nodes.statement:
As before, we analyze the evolution starting  at $t=r$ with $X_r=x$. Then if
$E_r=l$, $l > \varrho$,
  the drift will drive the
process out of the region through the {\it upper boundary\/} at time
$r+\varrho$. Otherwise  ($l \leqslant \varrho$) at least a jump
$J_{N_r+1}=-u$,  say, occurs at time $t_{N_r+1}$  before escape, and two possible scenarios appear depending on the relative magnitudes of the jump size and the location of the process right before the jump, $X_t=x+v l$: for $u\geqslant x+v l$ the
process will leave the interval through the {\it lower boundary\/} at $r+E_r$, but when $u<x+v l$ the process after the jump will remain inside the interval, $X_{r+l}=x+v l-u$, the exit problem will start afresh, and the mean escape time will be increased by $\mathbb{T}_b\left(x+v l-u\right)$.

nodes.statement_short: Otherwise a jump of size $-u$ exits through 0 if $u\ge x+vl$, else the problem restarts at $x+vl-u$.

nodes.name: Equations for mean exit times with opposite drift and jumps
nodes.statement:

that $T_b(x,r)$ and $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$ must satisfy for $0< x< b$
\begin{eqnarray}

\int^{\varrho}_{0} l
\phi(l|r) \int^{\infty}_{x+v l} h(u) d  ud  l \nonumber \\
+\int^{\varrho}_{0} \phi(l|r) \int^{x+vl}_{0} h(u)
 \left[l+\mathbb{T}_b\left(x+vl-u\right)\right]d  ud  l\nonumber \\
=
\int^{\varrho}_{0}\left[1-\Phi\left(l|r\right)\right]d  l \nonumber \\
+
\frac{1}{v}\int^{b}_{x}
\phi\left(\left.\frac{z-x}{v}\right|r\right) \int^{z}_{0} h(u)
\mathbb{T}_b\left(z-u\right)d  ud  z,\nonumber \\ \end{eqnarray}
\begin{eqnarray}
\mathbb{T}_b(x)= \int^{\varrho}_{0}\left[1-\Psi(l)\right]d  l
\nonumber \\
+\frac{1}{v} \int^{b}_{x} \psi\left(\frac{z-x}{v}\right)
\int^{z}_{0} h(u) \mathbb{T}_b\left(z-u\right)d  ud  z. \nonumber \\ \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Laplace solution with unknown constants A, B
nodes.statement:
We find a solution by Laplace transformation as
\begin{eqnarray}
\hat{ \mathbb{T} }(s)= \frac{2\lambda/s +   (B v-2 \lambda A)v  + A
v^2s}{\lambda^2[1-\hat{h}(s)]-2\lambda v s+ v^2s^2},
\end{eqnarray}
where   $A $ and  $B$ are 
$\mathbb{T}(0)$ and $\mathbb{T}'(0)$ respectively.

inversion, cf. Eq.~(\ref{def_m}), $\mathbb{T}(x)$ follows in terms of
$A$ and $B$. By requiring~(\ref{boundary}) 
we obtain a linear algebraic system for $A$ and $B$,
which upon solution yields $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$ in closed form.

nodes.name: Exponential jumps, opposite signs
nodes.statement:
To be specific we consider the case when jumps are also exponentially
distributed: $h(x)=\gamma e^{-\gamma x}$. Then we have~(\ref{h_hat}) 
and  $\hat{\mathbb{T}}(s)$ is the rational
function
\begin{eqnarray}
\hat{\mathbb{T}}(s)= \frac{(\gamma+s)[2\lambda + (B v-2 \lambda A)v s+ A
v^2s^2]}{s^2[\lambda(\lambda-2 \gamma v)+(\gamma v-2\lambda) v s+
v^2s^2]}. \end{eqnarray}
Upon re-scale  of constants the inverse Laplace transform
of~(\ref{LUps}) reads


\begin{eqnarray}
\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}-\gamma v\right)\mathbb{T}(x)\nonumber \\
=\tilde A  +  \gamma   x +
 \left[\frac{\lambda}{v^2}(\lambda-\lambda
\tilde A+   v\tilde  B) -\frac{\tilde B}{2}
\xi_{-}\right]\frac{e^{\xi_+ x}-1}{\xi_+(\xi_+-\xi_-)} \nonumber \\
- \left[\frac{\lambda}{v^2}(\lambda-\lambda\tilde  A+   v
\tilde B) -\frac{\tilde B}{2}\xi_{+}\right]\frac{e^{\xi_-
x}-1}{\xi_-(\xi_+-\xi_-)},\nonumber \\
\end{eqnarray}
with
\begin{equation}
\xi_{\pm}\equiv
\frac{\lambda}{v}-\frac{\gamma}{2}\pm\frac{\gamma}{2}\sqrt{1+\frac{4\lambda}{\gamma
v}}.\end{equation}

Unfortunately    the final  expressions for $\tilde A$ and $\tilde B$  after imposing~(\ref{boundary}) are not
  very illuminating so
 we   do not  transcribe them here. Sampling values for different
parameter specifications can be found in Fig.~\ref{E2_down}.

nodes.name: Two-sided jumps
nodes.statement:
We finally consider the general case corresponding to a jump
process where $J_n$ can take both signs and hence can    exit
$(0,b)$ through either of the boundaries.

nodes.name: Renewal argument for two-sided jumps
nodes.statement:
The relevant analysis
is similar to that of the last section if one incorporates  the
possibility of an upper exit due to a jump: If $E_r=l>\varrho$ the drift drives directly the process through the upper boundary. If $l\leqslant \varrho$ at least a jump occurs before the exit of the process. When the size $u$ of this jump is positive and $u\geqslant b-x-vl$ the process leaves the interval at time $r+E_r$ through the upper boundary, when $u\leqslant -(x+vl)<0$ the exit takes place through the lower boundary, otherwise the process remains inside the interval $(0,b)$ and the problem restarts.
nodes.statement_short: As in Section 4, condition on the excess life, adding the possibility of an upward exit by a positive jump.

nodes.name: Analogy with previous section
nodes.statement:
The relevant analysis
is similar to that of the last section if one incorporates  the
possibility of an upper exit due to a jump:

nodes.statement: If $E_r=l>\varrho$ the drift drives directly the process through the upper boundary.
nodes.statement_short: If $l>\varrho$ the drift exits through $b$.

nodes.statement: If $l\leqslant \varrho$ at least a jump occurs before the exit of the process. When the size $u$ of this jump is positive and $u\geqslant b-x-vl$ the process leaves the interval at time $r+E_r$ through the upper boundary, when $u\leqslant -(x+vl)<0$ the exit takes place through the lower boundary, otherwise the process remains inside the interval $(0,b)$ and the problem restarts.

\mathbb{T}_b\left(z+u\right)d  ud  z,

To gain some insight  we use the

$ h(x)= q h_+(x)  + p  h_-(x)$ where $p$ is the probability  that
a given jump be  negative, $q\equiv 1-p$  and

in the positive/negative regions, i.e.  $h_+(x)\equiv h(x)
\theta(x) \big/ q$, say.

and  apart from the factor $q$ in front of the second term they
resemble Eqs.~(\ref{Tb_up}) and~(\ref{TTb_up}); it follows that

We consider
\begin{eqnarray}
\mathbb{F}(y)= \int^{y/v}_{0}\left[1-\Psi(l)\right]d  l  \nonumber \\+

\int^{z}_{0} h(u) \mathbb{F}\left(z-u\right)d  ud  z, 
\end{eqnarray}
for $y\in \mathbb{R}^{+}$ which is again solvable  by means of a Laplace
transform; then $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$ follows from  $\mathbb{T}_b(x) =\mathbb{F}(b-x)$  for
$x\in (0,b)$. With the previous selection for $h(\cdot)$ and
$\psi(\cdot)$, Eq.~(\ref{h_hat}), and in terms of    $z=sv $

We first consider the case when   $\lambda
  =\gamma v$. Under this assumption  $\hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)$ has poles at

$z=z_j\equiv \lambda \left(q^{1/3} e^{2\pi ij/3}-1\right)$, $j\in\{1,2,3\}$, and  $z=0$.
